A1.justification: Both complete 23-page PDFs describe the same Neural-MedBench work. Text and rendered-page comparisons establish that pages 3–23, including Appendices A–G, are identical. Differences are confined to front matter and limited reflow on pages 1–2.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 13 VLMs and human participants, grader validation, and analysis of 100 incorrect responses (Table 2, Section 5, and Appendices E–G).

after.justification: v2 retains these original model evaluations, human results, grader validation, and quantitative and qualitative error analyses.

M1.justification: The case-curation pipeline, structured prompting, and hybrid clinician-calibrated GPT-4o/BERTScore evaluation procedure are unchanged (Sections 3–4 and Appendices A–C).

E1.justification: Both retain the same reported 120 cases and 200 tasks, clinical sources, task families, and difficulty levels. Coverage in the benchmark comparisons and appendix cases is also unchanged.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains the identical 13-model comparator set and Medical Student and Senior Physician baselines. Comparator participation in the figures and appendix cases is unchanged.

E3.justification: The zero-shot setup, prompts, metrics, temperature 0.7, top-p 0.95, and human evaluation with five participants per group are unchanged (Section 4 and Appendices B–C).

E4.justification: The analysis of 100 incorrect responses, grader-bias analysis, and representative failure cases are identical (Section 5.3 and Appendices E–G). No ablation, robustness test, or supplementary analysis is added or removed.

E5.justification: The stated 95% Wilson-interval procedure, GPT-4o seed 22, grader–clinician correlation reporting, and inter-rater agreement reporting are unchanged (Appendices C–F).

E6.justification: All numerical results and displayed case outcomes are unchanged. For example, Table 2 retains MedGemma-27B-it pass@1 scores of 30.0% for direct diagnosis and 18.3% for complex diseases; Section 5.3 retains 51% reasoning failures and 27% perceptual failures.

T1.justification: The Wilson-interval formula in Appendix D is identical. No mathematical definitions, assumptions, derivations, or proofs are added or revised.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same Two-Axis Evaluation Framework, Neural-MedBench contribution, and claims concerning the breadth–depth disconnect and predominance of reasoning failures.

C2.justification: Interpretations of model failures and specialization remain identical. The limitations concerning benchmark scale, human sample size, disease representation, domain shift, and grader bias are retained without revision (Section 6 and Appendices A and E–F).

D1.justification: Model identifiers, prompt templates, image encoding, decoding settings, curation details, and dataset/grader access statements are unchanged (Section 8 and Appendices A–C).

R1.justification: The cited works, bibliography, related-work discussion, and positioning relative to existing medical benchmarks and evaluation methods are identical.

P1.justification: v2 removes Lijun Wang, Yuanyuan Peng, and their Shenzhen hospital affiliation, renumbers the remaining affiliations, and updates the version/date stamp. Author superscripts are not consistently updated. Scientific prose and section organization are unchanged.

P2.justification: The shortened affiliation block shifts first-page content upward and moves one introductory line from page 2 to page 1. All figures, tables, appendix displays, and layouts on pages 3–23 are identical.

improvement.justification: Scientific content and appendix evidence are unchanged, but v2 introduces an affiliation-reference inconsistency: v1 lists affiliation 6 for Peking University, whereas v2 lists only affiliations 1–5 while retaining Shangyang Li’s superscript 6. This creates a small editorial accuracy decline without a demonstrated scientific improvement.
